extraction.name: Common Corpus
extraction.description: Common Corpus is the largest open dataset for language model pre-training, containing approximately 2 trillion tokens. The data is either uncopyrighted or under permissible licenses. It contains a wide variety of languages ranging from main European languages to low-resource ones, and includes a large portion of code data. The dataset is composed of six collections: Open Government, Open Culture, Open Science, Open Web, Open Code, and Open Semantic, covering diverse genres, time periods, and domains.
extraction.license: Public Domain, CC-By, MIT, CC-By-SA, Apache-2.0, BSD-3-Clause, Open license, BSD-2-Clause, CC-BY-4.0, CC0-1.0
extraction.creator: PleIAs, Paris, France
extraction.inLanguage: Multilingual (English, French, German, Spanish, Latin, Italian, Polish, Greek, Portuguese, Russian, and many others including low-resource languages)
extraction.citeAs: Pierre-Carl Langlais, Carlos Rosas Hinostroza, Mattia Nee, Catherine Amett, Pavel Chizhov, Eliot Krzystof Jones, Irène Girard, David Mach, Anastasia Stasenko, Ivan P. Yamshchikov. Common Corpus: The Largest Collection of Ethical Data for LLM Pre-Training. arXiv:2506.01732v1 [cs.CL], 2 Jun 2025.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Common Corpus was assembled from multiple open and permissively licensed sources across six collections: Open Government (financial, legal, and administrative data), Open Culture (cultural heritage datasets including monographs and periodicals), Open Science (scientific papers and documents via OpenAlex and other open archives), Open Code (code data from the Stack v1 and v2), Open Web (Wikipedia, Wikisource, YouTube Commons, StackExchange), and Open Semantic (Wikidata). Data was collected using APIs, large-scale dumps (Collections As Data initiatives), and standard retrieval methods. The collection has been an ongoing effort since 2024, with the current version released in February 2025.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Web API, Web Scraping, Document analysis, Software Collection, Manual Human Curator
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Data sources include: SEC annual reports (1993-2024), WTO documents (1995-2024), AMF documents, EU Tenders (TED), GATT Library (1946-1996), Europarl, Caselaw Access Project (1658-2020), CourtListener, EUR-lex, Eurovoc, French Open Data, USPTO (2019-2022), UN Digital Library, OECD data, digitized cultural heritage from French National Library (Gallica), Library of Congress, Europeana, New Zealand National Library, German Digital Library, Spanish Biblioteca Digital Hispánica, Dutch Delpher, OpenAlex scientific papers, arXiv, Stack v1 and v2 (code), Wikipedia, Wikisource, YouTube Commons (CC-By licensed videos), StackExchange, and Wikidata.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: Data spans from as early as 1618 (Europeana Newspapers) and January 1, 1946 (GATT Library) up to 2024 (SEC, WTO, AMF documents). Collection effort started in May 2023, with the current version released in February 2025.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Wikidata items and properties were translated into formal natural language sequences (e.g., 'Q41309 | P:27 | Q171150' becoming 'Franz Liszt country of citizenship Kingdom of Hungary'). Within each entry, all available translations are provided as consecutive blocks separated by a newline. PII was replaced with fictitious but realistic values rather than removed or tagged. OCR errors were corrected using the OCRonos model based on Llama 3 8B. Toxic content was either removed or synthetically rewritten without the harmful language using the Celadon classifier.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Text segmentation was performed using Segmentext, trained to be resilient to broken and unstructured texts with digitization artifacts. OCR quality was assessed using OCRoscope (based on cld2 language identification, measuring non-recognized 7-grams) and OCRerrcr (a DeBERTa-v2-style model with 400M parameters). OCR correction was performed using OCRonos (based on Llama 3 8B). PII was identified and replaced using Microsoft's Presidio with custom regular expression patterns (achieving 85% accuracy for phone numbers). Toxicity detection and filtering was performed using Celadon (a DeBERTa-v3-small model ~140M parameters trained on 2M annotated samples), identifying toxic content along five dimensions: race and origin-based bias, gender and sexuality-based bias, religious bias, ability bias, and violence and abuse. For Open Code: files were filtered by desired language/format extensions, non-permissible licenses were removed, files with 75%+ digits were removed, and sequences of carriage returns were normalized.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Rights verification for Open Culture data followed specific criteria: author life + 70 years for non-US authors (Berne Convention), all publications after 1884 treated as public domain for works where author could not be identified, publication + 95 years for US authors, and no additional digitization rights recognized. An internal data reconciliation pipeline based on Wikidata dumps was used to verify author death dates. License information for each document is included in metadata. Toxicity annotation used the Celadon classifier trained on 2M annotated samples across five dimensions of harmful content.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Microsoft Presidio (for PII detection), Celadon DeBERTa-v3-small model (for toxicity detection), OCRerrcr DeBERTa-v2-style model (for OCR error detection), OpenAlex API (for license filtering of scientific documents)
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Segmentext (text segmentation model), OCRoscope (OCR quality detection tool based on cld2), OCRerrcr (DeBERTa-v2-style model with 400M parameters for OCR error detection), OCRonos (Llama 3 8B-based OCR correction model), Microsoft Presidio (PII detection and replacement), Celadon (DeBERTa-v3-small ~140M parameters multilingual toxicity classifier), fastText (language identification model for language distribution computation), cld2 (language identification tool)
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: Common Corpus is described as an evolving resource reflecting the need for a continuous open infrastructure rather than a fixed dataset. HuggingFace ensures proper archiving of past versions for reproducibility. The dataset is available on HuggingFace as an aggregation of 10,000 parquet files. Ongoing data collection is continuing as part of the LLMs4EU project, with planned expansion to African languages (e.g., Swahili, Wolof, Bambara). The dataset was first published in March 2024, with the current version released in February 2025 for the Paris AI Summit.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Personally Identifiable Information (PII) including phone numbers, email addresses, and IP addresses was identified and replaced. PII removal was performed using Microsoft's Presidio. PII was replaced with fictitious but realistic values to preserve text format while protecting individual privacy, in compliance with GDPR regulations.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: Common Corpus aims to support the pre-training of fully open and auditable LLMs that comply with AI legislation and data security regulations, including EU AI regulations. It enables open science research on LLMs without legal uncertainty. The dataset contributes to making LLM development accessible beyond English-speaking audiences through multilingual coverage. It supports the development of language models for low-resource languages. The dataset has been acknowledged as one of the main deliverables of the Paris AI Summit 2025 as the 'largest open database to train Large Language Models'. It serves as open science infrastructure for the entire lifecycle of language models as defined by UNESCO.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Historical texts in Open Culture (from the 18th-19th centuries or earlier) may contain language that does not meet modern ethical standards, including biased discussions of ethnic groups, women, and themes such as violence. A toxicity detection and filtering pipeline (Celadon) was developed to address this. The Open Science collection has less linguistic diversity with nearly 85% of documents in English due to the specificity of open scientific publishing. Low-resource language coverage is still shallow despite the large overall language diversity.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Common Corpus does not collect the full range of available open data (termed the 'open data paradox'). Coverage for low-resource languages is still shallow. The 2 trillion tokens is suitable for pre-training models of limited size; larger models will require significantly more data. The dataset does not contain data for instruction-tuning or specialized tasks, making it not directly suitable for task-specific fine-tuning. None of the curation methods can facilitate 100% accuracy. OCR errors may still be present in some documents. License identification for web-crawled content remains challenging. The multilingual data was never machine-translated, which limits coverage but ensures authenticity.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Primary use case is LLM pre-training. The dataset can be used on its own or in conjunction with existing open datasets. Specific use cases include: training multilingual language models, developing historical language models, training models for creative writing, developing vision-language models (VLMs) for document segmentation and processing, training models with legal knowledge, improving model performance on coding, natural language reasoning, mathematics, and structured output tasks. The dataset has been used to create multimodal datasets, classifiers, synthetic datasets, and benchmarks. It is not suitable for instruction-tuning or task-specific fine-tuning directly. Each data object contains license, language, collection/domain, and other metadata allowing filtering for desired subsets.
